title: Reading examiner reports
examples: How can I use this report to study better?
What does 'needs more depth' actually mean?
Should I worry about the negative comments?

explain.say: Examiner reports show how you scored on an exam.
They point out common errors students often make.
Top answers show what examiners look for in great work.
When you read the report, look for patterns in the feedback.
In real life, reading a report helps you plan your next steps.
A common mistake is only reading the final grade given.

faq.q: What is the main purpose of an examiner report?
faq.a: It gives you detailed feedback on your performance. It shows you exactly where you scored well and where you need to improve your understanding.
asks: What do these reports tell me?
What should I look for in the feedback?

faq.q: How do I know if my answer is good enough?
faq.a: Compare your answer to the examples of top work provided. See what specific details they included that you missed.
asks: What level of detail is expected?

faq.q: If I see 'needs more depth', what should I do?
faq.a: It means you need to explain your ideas with more detail. Try adding examples or reasons to support your main points.
asks: What does 'depth' mean in this context?
How can I add more detail?

faq.q: Should I focus only on the mistakes I made?
faq.a: No, look at everything. The positive comments tell you what you are already doing well. Use those strengths too.
asks: Should I ignore the good parts?
Is it okay to focus only on errors?

faq.q: Are examiner reports the same for every exam?
faq.a: No, they are specific to the subject and the exam board. Always read the instructions for that particular test.
asks: Does this apply to all subjects?

facts: Examiner reports provide specific feedback on student work.
Top answers demonstrate depth and use specific evidence.
Common errors are patterns of mistakes, not just single slips.
The report helps you create a targeted study plan.

quiz.say: A report says your answer is 'too general'. This means you should:

options.show: Repeat the question in your answer.
options.say: Repeat the question in your answer.

options.show: Provide concrete evidence to support your claims.
options.say: Provide concrete evidence to support your claims.

quiz.why: This shows the examiner you have researched the topic deeply.

wrong.0: Using big words does not automatically make the answer better.
wrong.1: Length alone does not guarantee quality understanding.
wrong.2: This wastes valuable space and does not answer the prompt.

quiz.say: If you see 'lacks analysis', you should focus on:

options.show: Explaining the causes and effects of the topic.
options.say: Explaining the causes and effects of the topic.

quiz.why: Analysis means breaking down ideas to see how they connect.

wrong.0: This avoids the difficult part of explaining the connections.
wrong.2: Listing facts only describes; it does not explain the 'why'.
wrong.3: A summary just repeats what was already said.

quiz.say: When comparing your work to a top answer, what is the most useful thing to note?

options.show: The color of the ink used.
options.say: The color of the ink used.

options.show: The specific vocabulary or terminology used.
options.say: The specific vocabulary or terminology used.

quiz.why: Using precise subject language shows you know the field well.

wrong.0: Length is secondary to the quality of the ideas presented.
wrong.1: The ink color has no bearing on academic assessment.
wrong.3: The examiner cares about your ideas, not your penmanship.
